newsitem.title: USA: Lower Mississippi falls, but shipping curbs remain.
newsitem.headline: Lower Mississippi falls, but shipping curbs remain.

text.p: The Coast Guard said Wednesday swift currents are slowing down and water levels continue to recede on the lower Mississippi River, but shipping regulations will remain in place until the swollen river subsides further.

"Things are calming down, it's not as tense," said Lieutenant Matt Jones of the New Orleans Coast Guard Marine Safety Office, adding that no serious mishaps have occurred this week on the accident-prone river stretch between Baton Rouge and New Orleans.
He said water levels in New Orleans have retreated in the past week to 16.2 feet, about 0.8 foot below official flood mark -- a sharp improvement from the 16.9-foot heights seen a week ago.
Although the river Wednesday remained well above the 35-foot flood stage in Baton Rouge, at 40.9 feet, it had dipped four inches since Tuesday.

"She's still a little swift but every day she drops she's better," said a spokesman for the Vessel Traffic System, a quasi-government group helping the Port of Baton Rouge monitor shipping following a series of barge accidents attributed to fast currents over the past few weeks.

Authorities said the river is flowing at a speed of about six knots near Baton Rouge, about two knots faster than normal but far safer than eight-knot speeds that made navigation so perilous early last week.

Lt. Jones said shipping regulations remain unchanged, including a daytime-only restriction on all southbound, deep-draft vessels carrying certain volatile chemicals and compressed gases from Mile 233 near Baton Rouge to just south of New Orleans.
Petroleum products such as gasoline were not subject to the daytime-only requirement.
In addition, strict minimum horsepower requirements for tow boats remain in place, including one requiring all southbound tows with greater than 25 barges to have 8,000-brake horsepower.
Draft limits imposed at the mouth of the Mississippi permit drafts up to 44 feet for vessels less than 100,000 tonnes. Ships exceeding 100,000 tonnes are limited to drafts of 43 feet.
((- Ransdell Pierson, New York Energy Desk, 212 859-1632))
